beats.care: Whatever AI app you use, assume what you type may be stored on the company's servers. Keep passwords, ID numbers and private files out.
beats.what: The US Department of Homeland Security ordered federal civilian agencies to stop buying DeepSeek products and remove them from their systems.
beats.why: US officials say Chinese law could let authorities access data that government users type into DeepSeek's tools.

cards.body: The order also cites a 2025 security report on DeepSeek's iPhone app that found weak encryption and data being sent without encryption.

a.body: Chinese authorities could access sensitive government data and track users, so the tools are a national security risk.
a.label: US officials say

b.body: Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said the US is overstretching national security and politicising technology and trade.
b.label: China says

cards.body: DeepSeek is open-source, so many other apps quietly run on its models. That is why the ban reaches third-party products too.

opts: Fear data could reach China's government
cards.q: Why did the US order DeepSeek off its agencies' systems?
cards.why: Officials worry Chinese law could let Beijing get data that government staff type into the AI.

hook: The US just kicked DeepSeek off *government computers*. What's the fear?

learn.t: The order covers apps built on DeepSeek's AI too, not just DeepSeek's own app, and doesn't stop ordinary Americans using it.

tldr: The US ordered its civilian government agencies to remove Chinese AI company DeepSeek's products, including apps built on it.
watch: US agencies have 60 days to ask for exceptions, which the cyber agency CISA will approve or reject.
